summary: This standards-track RFC extends IS-IS to advertise node administrative tags. They group and tag nodes in an IS-IS domain so locally defined policies can use them, by IS-IS or other applications.

eli5.summary: Sticky notes on routers so network rules can say all routers with this note.

questions: what is an is-is node administrative tag
how are node admin tags flooded in is-is
does the order of node admin tags matter
subtitle: A way for IS-IS routers to carry 32-bit group labels that network policies can match on.

tldr.problem: Operators want to group routers in an IS-IS domain (for example edge versus core) so local policies can treat each group differently, but IS-IS had no standard way to advertise such a label for a node.
tldr.mechanism: A new Node-Admin-Tag sub-TLV, carried inside the Router CAPABILITY TLV, lists one or more 32-bit unsigned administrative tags for the originating router.
tldr.outcome: Routers flood the tags, and policies and applications such as path selection or Loop-Free Alternate pruning can use them. IS-IS itself treats the tag values as opaque.

today: RFC 7917 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The OSPF counterpart is RFC 7777.

sections.title: Why Tag Nodes
sections.content:
It is useful to assign a node administrative tag to a router in an IS-IS domain and use it as an attribute of that node. The RFC gives two example uses: traffic-engineering applications that want different path-selection criteria, and preferring or pruning certain paths in Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) backup selection through local policies, as defined in RFC 7916.

Because route and path selection applies to both traffic-engineering (TE) and non-TE uses, the new sub-TLV is placed in the Router CAPABILITY TLV from RFC 4971.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the network owner wants to say 'these routers are special'. A tag is a label on a router that lets the rules pick them out.

sections.title: What an Administrative Tag Is
sections.content:
An administrative tag is a 32-bit unsigned integer that identifies a group of nodes in the IS-IS domain. A router should advertise, in the specific IS-IS level, the set of groups it belongs to.

The RFC's example: all edge devices in a network may be configured with one tag value, and all core devices with a different one.
sections.eli5: A tag is just a number, like a team number on a jersey. All edge routers might wear one number and all core routers another.

sections.title: The Node-Admin-Tag Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The sub-TLV is carried in an IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV (IS-IS TLV type 242) in the Link State PDUs the device originates. It has Type 21 (Node-Admin-Tag), an 8-bit Length giving the size of the value in octets, and a value made of one or more 4-octet tags. The length is therefore a multiple of 4.

Router CAPABILITY TLVs can have level-wide or domain-wide flooding scope. Which scope a given tag is flooded in is purely a matter of local policy. An operator MAY advertise one set of tags across levels and a different set within a specific level, or use the same tags in both.

The sub-TLV has no topology identifier, so tags cannot be advertised per topology. In multi-topology routing deployments, advertising a separate set of tags for each topology SHOULD NOT be supported.
sections.eli5: The message is a little list: a label saying 'these are tags', how long the list is, then the tag numbers one after another. The network owner decides how far the list travels.

sections.title: Rules for Using and Processing Tags
sections.content:
The meaning of a tag is generally opaque to IS-IS. It is defined by network local policy and set by configuration. A router can advertise a tag without knowing what functionality it implies. Tag values SHOULD NOT be propagated outside the administrative domain they apply to. A receiver that does not understand a tag ignores it and floods the Router CAPABILITY TLV unchanged.

The order of tags has no meaning. Each tag SHOULD be treated as an independent identifier, and the list MUST be considered unordered. Policies may combine tags (tag A AND tag B), but they MUST NOT depend on order.

Tags are not meant to be extended by future IS-IS standards and need no IANA registration. They are expected to describe a stable attribute: they MUST NOT be tied to something that can oscillate frequently, such as the reachability of a destination. No limit on the number of tags is defined, but only a modest number is expected to be needed.

Several Node-Admin-Tag sub-TLVs MAY appear in one Router CAPABILITY TLV or across different instances of it. The tags a receiver uses for a node SHOULD be the superset of all tags from all those TLVs. When the set changes, a receiving node MUST repeat any computation that uses the tags, and an originating node whose affiliation changes MUST re-originate its Router CAPABILITY TLV(s) with the latest set.
sections.eli5: The tags are like a bag of stickers: the order does not matter, and a router that does not know what a sticker means just passes it along. If a router gets new stickers, everyone redoes their rules.

sections.title: Applications and Operations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 7777, which covers the same idea for OSPF, for non-normative examples: auto-discovery of services, policy-based Fast Reroute (limiting LFA scope and optimizing LFA calculations), controlling remote LFA tunnel termination, mobile backhaul service deployment, and policy-based explicit routing. An implementation is not required to support any of these use cases.

Operationally, tags are analogous to IS-IS prefix tags and BGP communities, and the same operational discipline applies. Defining a policy language is out of scope. The RFC warns that pruning policies can remove a path from the forwarding plane entirely, which can have a more severe impact (such as node unreachability) than preference policies that only affect path selection.

Tags are expected to be configured through routing policy and YANG models, which at the time of writing were still being extended for this purpose.
sections.eli5: Tags can help with things like choosing backup routes. But a rule that throws a path away is riskier than a rule that just prefers one path, so be careful.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security issues. Like link administrative tags, node tags can be used to indicate geographical location or other sensitive information, and that information can leak to an IGP snooper.

Advertising tag values from one administrative domain into another risks misinterpretation if the two domains gave different meanings to the same values. Existing IS-IS security (ISO 10589, RFC 5304, RFC 5310) applies, and the extended authentication in the latter two SHOULD be used where attackers can reach the physical network.
sections.eli5: A tag can give away secrets, like where a router sits, to anyone listening. Also, your 'red sticker' might mean something else in someone else's network.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC updates one IS-IS registry, the 'Sub-TLVs for TLV 242' registry, with value 21 for Node-Admin-Tag. It does not create any registry for tag values themselves.
sections.eli5: The official list of message parts got one new entry, number 21, for node tags.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in octets, a multiple of 4.

fields.name: Administrative Tag #1 (first 16 bits)
fields.desc: First part of the first 32-bit tag.

fields.name: Administrative Tag #1 (last 16 bits) and further tags
fields.desc: Rest of tag #1, then tag #2 through tag #N, each 4 octets.
